title: Redlines Structure Profile
description: Schema for a redlines structure profile: the declarative format (ADR-0006, ADR-0028) that tells a reader how to recognise labels, headings, roles and semantic spans in a document family. Files are YAML on disk; this schema describes the mapping shape after parsing, which is the same shape a profile passed as a Python dict or MCP tool argument must have. Every 'pattern' in this schema is Python `re` syntax, so inline flags like (?i) and lookarounds are available. In YAML, write patterns as single-quoted scalars ('...') so backslashes stay literal and need no doubling; a pattern containing an apostrophe doubles it ('parties'' case') rather than switching to double quotes, which would force every backslash to be doubled too.

name.description: The profile's name, used to select it explicitly (R1d).

description.description: A short, human-readable description of the document family this profile targets.

label_patterns.description: Patterns recognising a leading label on a paragraph or list item, tried in order. Order is precedence: the first pattern that matches wins.

heading_resets.description: Headings that open a new section and clear the label-depth stack (e.g. Schedule, Annex, Part), which is what keeps alpha/roman labels unambiguous after the boundary. This is only about numbering: a reset does not assign a role, and a role_rule does not clear the stack. A profile that wants both from the same heading declares it in both lists, which is why the worked example repeats one regex. Only headings listed here touch the stack: every other heading leaves the numbering alone, so a document whose paragraph numbering runs continuously from start to finish simply declares no resets.

heading_rule.description: General heuristics for recognising a short, unlabelled line as a heading. These narrow the field of candidates; they are not the whole scorer, and the reader weighs other signals (surrounding blank lines, indentation, what follows) that a profile does not control. A short sentence-case line can still be scored as a heading with both case flags left on -- the flags admit candidates rather than excluding everything else.

role_rules.description: Rules assigning a semantic role (ADR-0005) to blocks, tried in order. A block carries one role, so order is precedence: the first rule that matches wins and the rest are not tried. Roles are assigned walking the block tree top-down, so a block's ancestors already carry their roles by the time its own rules are tried -- which is what makes a 'parent_role' rule work. List the rule that assigns a role before any rule that depends on it as a parent_role. Proximity beats list order: 'ancestor_heading' rules are resolved from the block outwards, so the nearest matching ancestor heading decides, and list order only breaks a tie between rules matching that same heading. A 'Conclusion' section nested inside 'My decision' therefore gives its paragraphs the conclusion role, however the two rules are ordered.

span_extractors.description: Regexes extracting semantic spans (ADR-0005) -- defined terms, cross-references, parties, dates, amounts -- from block text. Unlike label_patterns and role_rules, order is not precedence: a block carries many spans, so every extractor runs and all matches are kept. Order only fixes the order the spans are emitted in. Two extractors may share a type -- several unrelated patterns for one kind of span is the expected way to write this, not a mistake.

name.description: A short, plain name for this pattern (e.g. 'decimal', 'alpha_paren').

pattern.description: A regular expression matching the label at the start of the block text.

style.description: The label's numbering style. 'decimal' is a dotted or bare number ('1', '1.2.3') and carries its own depth from the dot-separated groups. 'alpha' ('(a)', 'A.') and 'roman' ('(i)', 'IV.') are ambiguous in isolation -- '(i)' after '(h)' is alphabetic, after '7.2' it is roman -- and are resolved by depth_mode. 'word' is a label introduced by a word ('Article 5', 'Section 3', 'Schedule 2', 'Part IV').

depth_mode.description: 'arithmetic': depth is counted from the label itself (e.g. '1.2.3' is depth 3, a bare '17' is depth 1). 'stack': depth is resolved from the label-style stack, for styles that are ambiguous on their own. The two share one stack, so an arithmetic label sets the level a following stack-mode label nests under -- which is how '(a)' after '7.2' lands one level deeper than '(a)' after '7'.

name.description: A short, plain name for this reset (e.g. 'schedule').

pattern.description: A regular expression matching the heading text that triggers the reset.

max_words.description: A line longer than this many words is never scored as a heading. Words are whitespace-separated tokens of the heading text after any label is stripped, so the label does not count against the budget and "parties'" counts as one word.

allow_all_caps.description: Score an all-caps short line as a heading candidate.

allow_title_case.description: Score a title-case short line as a heading candidate.

forbid_terminal_punctuation.description: A line ending in terminal punctuation (. ; :) is never scored as a heading.

role.description: The semantic role to assign. The vocabulary is open (ADR-0005): any string is accepted and nothing in the library enforces a list, so a document family can name a role of its own. The recommended set -- title, recital, definition, clause, sub_clause, schedule, signature, note, quote, code, boilerplate -- is what renderers, filters and the change tree already understand, so prefer it where one fits and invent a name only where none does.

match.description: 'heading': the block is itself a heading whose text matches pattern. 'ancestor_heading': the block sits somewhere under a heading matching pattern, at any depth. 'parent_role': the block's immediate parent in the block tree -- the block that contains it, which for a block directly under a heading is that heading's block -- already carries the role named in parent_role. Use 'ancestor_heading' to match on a heading's text and 'parent_role' to build on a role another rule already assigned; 'parent_role' is the only one of the three that looks at depth 1 exactly. Choose between 'heading' and 'ancestor_heading' by what you want the role to land on: 'heading' labels the heading block itself, so filters and renderers see the heading; 'ancestor_heading' labels the content underneath it and not the heading. A profile that wants both writes both rules. All three match kinds are structural -- none of them looks at the block's own text.

pattern.description: Required when match is 'heading' or 'ancestor_heading'; must not be set otherwise. Matched against the heading's text with any label already stripped, so '^Background' matches the heading '3. Background'.

parent_role.description: Required when match is 'parent_role'; must not be set otherwise.

type.description: The span type (ADR-0005 recommends: emphasis, defined_term, cross_reference, party, date, amount, citation).

pattern.description: A regular expression searched for anywhere in the block's text, as many times as it matches -- unlike label and heading patterns, which are tried at the start. Anchor it yourself if you mean the start.

group.description: Which capturing group of pattern is the span's text; 0 is the whole match. Omit it entirely for a pattern with no capturing groups. A span is a typed range of text, not a structured record -- there is one group and no attributes -- so a citation captured as a single span keeps the text as written rather than splitting it into parts.
